title: Written On the Same Rock
logline: One face of granite in a ruined medieval capital carries colossal carved figures and, between two of them, fifty-one lines of small writing: the settlement of a quarrel a thousand years old, set down not as an account of anybody's mind but as a list of what may and may not be done.
human_question: When a long quarrel is finally settled, the settlement is written down as rules — so what happened to everything that was actually in the people who were quarrelling?

place.what_kind_of_place: One rock face, and nothing else. A long outcrop of dark granite at the northern edge of a ruined medieval capital in the dry zone, worked in the twelfth century into four colossal images cut from the living stone — a large seated figure, a small seated one inside an excavated cave, a standing figure with its arms crossed on its chest, and a reclining figure longer than a bus. Between the cave's doorway and the standing figure, a rectangle of the same rock has been ground flat and polished and then filled, edge to edge, with fifty-one lines of medieval Sinhala writing in letters small enough to need a step forward to see. The images and the writing are on one continuous surface, cut by one work programme, and the film never leaves it. It is not a ruin: the face is a working place of worship, with a paved terrace in front of it, shoes and hats off, a rope line, and a slow constant traffic of visitors and pilgrims all day. A large modern metal shelter stands over the whole face to keep the weather off the carving.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because one frame can hold the largest and the smallest thing anybody made here. A standing figure of nearly seven metres and, a couple of paces to its right, writing a few millimetres high — and both of them are the same rock, cut by the same people in the same decade. Sound off, the film is a study of one surface at two scales: the enormous, calm, wet-looking sheen of granite worked to a curve; the grain and the quartz and the lichen; feet on hot pale paving; and then macro, at the end of a long lens or a diopter, where the whole screen is filled by four letters and the shadow inside the cut of one of them. There is no landscape in this film, no drone, no horizon, no weather beyond what comes in sideways under the shelter, and almost no camera movement — every shot is locked off, and the only things that move are light and people. The reward for that discipline is a texture film of unusual intensity: a viewer who never hears a word gets stone, scale, letterform and light, and one long final push into a surface until the writing stops being writing and becomes marks.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Nothing on the rock changes at all, which is the point and has to be filmed as such. What changes is the light and the people. Under the shelter the face is in permanent shade with a bright edge, so the usable light arrives sideways in the first hour after the gates open and again late in the afternoon, and it crosses the inscribed panel at a shallow angle for a short time and then stops. The crowd thickens from mid-morning, thins at midday heat, and comes back before closing. Offerings are set down and taken away. Bare feet change the sound. Over the length of a day the writing goes from readable-in-places to a flat grey field and back, and the film is structured on that: the letters appear and disappear on a schedule nobody controls.
place.when_it_looks_best: Two separate windows on the same day, and they are for different things. Early, from the moment the site opens, for low sideways light reaching in under the shelter across the inscribed panel — the only time the cutting reads at all. Late afternoon for the same reason from the other side, and for the warm bounce off the paving onto the images. The middle of the day is for the colossal figures in flat shade, which suits them, and for the crowd. The dry months give the cleanest air and the hardest light; a bright overcast day is better for the carving and worse for the letters. If the panel does not read in whatever light the day gives, the film says so and shows it not reading.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about one surface. It opens on a held wide frame of a single rock face in first light — colossal figures, a cave doorway, and a pale rectangle of writing between them — and then works inwards for forty minutes without ever cutting away to anything else: the standing figure's crossed hands, the join where a carved robe meets uncut stone, the polished panel from an angle so that fifty-one lines rise out of the grain, then a single line, then a single letter, then the shadow in the bottom of one stroke. People come and go at the edge of frame and are never the subject. It ends where it began, on the whole face, with the light gone flat and the writing invisible again. Anyone who hears no narration gets a complete piece with a shape: the biggest thing here and the smallest thing here, and the discovery that they are the same rock.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes an argument about what a record can and cannot hold. The voice explains that the small writing is a code of conduct drawn up when a division in the monastic order roughly a thousand years old was brought to an end, and that a quarrel between religious houses is exactly the place where the old lists of unwholesome mental factors — envy, stinginess, conceit, wrong view — would be alleged to have been living. Then it does the thing the footage was built for: it shows that what actually survives on this rock is not a description of anybody's mind but a schedule of what may be done, when, and by whom. The second concept supplies the sharp end. The books say these factors combine under strict rules — conceit and wrong view can never be in one mind, envy and stinginess and regret never arrive together — so a quarrel described as all of those at once was never a mind at all; it was an enormous number of separate moments in an enormous number of people, and not one of them is on the stone. The film's honest limit is written into it rather than appended: a code of conduct proves a dispute existed and proves nothing whatever about what was in anyone, the sources themselves say no outside observer can tell which factor is present, and the inscription, near its end, forbids speaking ill of anyone for performing these duties unwillingly. The stone regulates the doing and declines to read the doer. So does the film.

sequence.on_screen: Locked-off wide frame, first light, the whole rock face in one shot: a large seated figure, a cave doorway, a standing figure, and between the doorway and the standing figure a paler rectangle of rock. No movement in the shot at all except a shaft of low light crossing the paving.
sequence.voice: Everything in this film is on one rock. Four figures cut out of the living stone, the tallest of them nearly seven metres. And between two of them, a patch of rock that was ground flat, polished, and then covered in writing so small you have to walk up to it.

sequence.on_screen: A step closer, still locked off. The polished panel filling the frame at an oblique angle so that the lines of script lift out of the grain. Then a slow macro rack down two or three lines of letters.
sequence.voice: Fifty-one lines. The first part is a history and the rest is a set of rules. It was cut for Parakramabahu, who ruled in the twelfth century, after the monastic order, divided into three fraternities — Mahavihara, Abhayagiri and Jetavana — was brought back into one. The stone gives the length of the division in its own arithmetic: one thousand two hundred and fifty-four years. It also speaks in the king's own voice, and it does not undersell him: seeing a blot on the religion, a mighty emperor like myself cannot remain indifferent. That is the stone's wording about itself, not a verdict anyone else reached.

sequence.on_screen: Macro, very shallow focus, travelling along one line of script. Then a pull back just far enough to show the panel's edge, where the polished rectangle stops and the raw granite starts.
sequence.voice: A quarrel between religious houses is exactly where the old lists would expect to find their material. Fourteen unwholesome mental factors are named, in the same order in both books: delusion, shamelessness, no dread of wrongdoing, restlessness, greed, wrong view, conceit, hate, envy, stinginess, remorse, sloth, torpor, doubt [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3]. Envy looks outward, at somebody else's standing, and the older commentary says one of the things it does is take people who keep the precepts and paint their virtue as hypocrisy, a device for getting gifts and honours [C022-P:L129].

sequence.on_screen: The standing figure's crossed forearms and chest, held, filling the frame; then the same lens length on the inscribed panel, so the two surfaces are cut together at the same scale.
sequence.voice: Stinginess looks the other way, at one's own [C022-P:L133], and the list of what it fastens on is uncomfortably close to what three monastic houses had: a dwelling, a following, a gain, appearance, and the teaching itself [C022-P:L135; C022-M:L45]. Conceit is mis-measuring one's own standing, and one of its named kinds is measuring yourself by your own discipline and concentration [C022-P:L103; C022-P:L107]. Wrong view is holding facts against reason and conditions [C022-P:L91]. A dispute about discipline and doctrine at once is a dispute made of exactly these words.

sequence.on_screen: Extreme macro: one letter, so close that the stroke is a valley with a lit wall and a dark floor. Dust in the cut. Then a very slow, almost imperceptible drift out to four letters.
sequence.voice: And then the second list does something nobody expects. It does not only name the factors; it says which of them can be in a mind at the same moment. Conceit and wrong view both grow out of wanting, and they can never occupy one mind together, because they are two different grips — this is how things are, against this is how I rank [C026-P:L35; C026-M:L17]. Envy, stinginess and regret each need displeasure to arise at all, and never arrive with one another; one at a time, or not at all [C026-P:L39].

sequence.on_screen: Back to the full panel, shot square on in flatter light so that the writing is barely legible. Then, at the edge of frame, bare feet crossing hot paving; then the panel again, empty.
sequence.voice: So a quarrel described as envious and grasping and proud and wrong-headed all at once was never one mind. These factors live only in twelve kinds of mind and in none of the other seventy-seven [C026-P:L25], and four of them are in every single one of those twelve [C026-P:L29]. Each of the rest is a single moment that excludes its neighbours, so what a thousand years of division actually consisted of was an enormous number of separate moments in an enormous number of people. The combination the books describe happens invisibly, one flicker at a time. The combination this rock records is administrative. What is cut here is when a monk may walk to the village, what he must learn by heart, that he may not be angry with a servant without going to the elders first, and that a dispute being settled in one monastery is not to be carried outside it.

sequence.on_screen: A long lens down the last few lines of the inscription, where the writing runs to the bottom edge of the polished rectangle and stops. Hold.
sequence.voice: The record says that hundreds of monks were removed from the order, and the code sets out how: warned, punished, warned again, three times, then a month, and then out, with no one to keep company with him. That is what the stone says, and this film says it once and leaves it. Because a few lines earlier the same code says something it is very hard to improve on. No ill is to be spoken of anyone for performing these duties unwillingly.

sequence.on_screen: The slowest move in the film: a single continuous pull back from one letter to the whole face, ending on the opening frame with the light gone flat and the panel now a blank grey rectangle.
sequence.voice: It regulates the doing and refuses to read the doer, and a camera can do nothing better. Nothing cut into this rock tells you whether one monk on one morning felt envy, or conceit, or nothing at all; the books are explicit that these factors are not visible from outside. The older text allows for that, too: uncertainty about a matter you do not know is not the doubt on the list of faults [C022-P:L179]. So this is what there is. A surface with the largest thing on it and the smallest thing on it, and a settlement written as rules because rules are the only part of a quarrel that can be carved.

concept_merge.why_together: C022 supplies the vocabulary that a monastic quarrel would be described in, and it supplies it with unusual precision: fourteen factors in a fixed order in both sources [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3], envy defined as taking other people's standing as its object and disparaging the virtuous as hypocrites after gifts [C022-P:L129], stinginess defined as taking one's own and fastening on five things — a dwelling, a following, a gain, appearance and the teaching [C022-P:L133; C022-P:L135; C022-M:L45] — conceit defined as mis-measuring one's own standing, with discipline and concentration among the things people measure themselves by [C022-P:L103; C022-P:L107], and wrong view defined as holding facts against reason and conditions [C022-P:L91]. Those five are a near-exact inventory of what a dispute between three monastic houses over discipline, doctrine, residence and patronage would be alleged to contain. C022 alone, though, would produce an accusation dressed as a film. C026 is what turns it into an argument, because C026 is the rulebook for combination: the fourteen occur only in twelve minds and nowhere else [C026-P:L25], four of them are in every one of those twelve [C026-P:L29; C026-M:L15], conceit and wrong view can never share a mind because they are different modes of grasping [C026-P:L35; C026-M:L17], and envy, stinginess and remorse each require aversion and never arrive together [C026-P:L39]. Read properly, that is a statement about arithmetic: the four or five things a quarrel gets accused of cannot be one state. They can only be a very large number of separate, momentary, mutually exclusive states, distributed across a very large number of people and a very long time. And the one thing this rock face holds is a code — a list of permissions and prohibitions, drawn up by named elders after a congregation, cut on the same stone as the colossal images.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the settlement of a quarrel and the contents of a quarrel are two different objects, and only one of them can be written on a rock. The pairing produces the film's single best frame and its argument in the same shot: a figure nearly seven metres high and letters a few millimetres high, on one surface, cut by one work programme — the scale at which a monastic order does things, and the scale at which the record of its discipline is kept. It also gives the film an unusually honest ending, because the ending is in the source rather than in our commentary. The code's own provisions include a rule against speaking ill of anyone who performs the duties unwillingly; the digests say plainly that no camera and no observer can show which mental factor is present; and the Pradeepika allows that not knowing a thing you do not know is not the unwholesome doubt [C022-P:L179]. Three independent refusals to read a mind from outside, one of them cut into the rock in the twelfth century. Neither concept alone reaches that: C022 by itself names faults and would be tempted to allocate them, and C026 by itself is a table of co-occurrence with nothing in front of it.

concept_links.why: The digest's own inventory is what makes this rock face a concept rather than a monument. Both sources give the same fourteen factors in the same order [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3], and Pradeepika is the one that marks the first four as present in all twelve unwholesome minds while Margaya leaves that to a later section [C022-P:L31]. Four of the remaining ten are named in terms that map onto a documented dispute between monastic houses without any stretching: envy takes other people's prosperity and standing as its object, and is described as disparaging those who keep precepts and meditate by presenting their virtue as hypocrisy and as a device for obtaining gifts and honours [C022-P:L129]; stinginess takes one's own as its object [C022-P:L133] and fastens on five things, among them a dwelling, a following, a gain, appearance and the teaching itself [C022-P:L135; C022-M:L45]; conceit is mis-measuring one's own standing, with birth, discipline and merit named among the measures [C022-P:L103; C022-P:L107]; and wrong view is the habit of holding matters contrary to reason and conditions [C022-P:L91]. The film uses those definitions to say what a quarrel would be alleged to contain, and then refuses to allege it. Several of the digest's limits are load-bearing rather than decorative here, and each is written into the film or the risks. The digest flags that Margaya's fourth aspect of stinginess reads as 'indicating' one's own attainments where Pradeepika has 'not bearing others to know of it', and suspects an OCR error needing checking against the print [C022-M:L43]; the film therefore rests nothing at all on the 'cannot bear it to be known' aspect, even though a settled dispute over monastic property appears to offer it. The digest also rules out 'putting yourself down is humility' as a way of moralising about low self-worth [C022-P:L111], and warns that the description of equal-conceit contains egalitarian-sounding statements that must not be quoted against social equality [C022-P:L109] — a live danger in a film about three houses being made into one, and the reason the voice never uses the three-directions material at all. Finally the digest's line on doubt is used positively and in its own sense: ordinary uncertainty about something one does not know is not the fault the list means [C022-P:L179], which is exactly the position the film ends in.

This is the concept that turns an inscription into an argument, because it is about combination and the film is about what a combination looks like when it is written down. Pradeepika restricts all fourteen to the twelve unwholesome minds and excludes them from the other seventy-seven [C026-P:L25], makes the delusion tetrad certain in all twelve [C026-P:L29], states that conceit and wrong view cannot occupy one mind because each is as strong as the other [C026-P:L35], and states that envy, stinginess and remorse arise only with aversion, only occasionally, and never two of them at once [C026-P:L39]. Margaya supplies the reasons: the two graspings are different in kind, permanence-and-self against superiority [C026-M:L17]; every unwholesome mind requires delusion hiding the danger, shamelessness, no dread and agitation, and cannot arise at all while wisdom sees the fault or shame and dread are awake or the mind rests on something good [C026-M:L15]; and stinginess, though it grows out of attachment to one's own, arises with aversion rather than greed, because what it consists of is displeasure at sharing [C026-M:L19]. The film's central claim rests on the co-occurrence rules and nothing else: a dispute characterised as envious and proud and doctrinally fixed cannot be a state, only a distribution of momentary states. The digest's own limits are honoured on screen rather than in a footnote. 'A psychological formula for reading people' is precisely what the film must not become, and its closing beat says a camera cannot show which factor is present. 'Bad people are shameless' is refused, because the four constant factors describe every unwholesome moment in anyone and not a type of person [C026-M:L15] — which is why the film never sorts the historical parties into the disciplined and the corrupt. 'Stinginess is greed' is the English equation the sources reject [C026-M:L19], so the film does not call the monastic holdings greed. And 'being pushed excuses it' is refused too [C026-P:L43], which matters here, because a code enforced by a king is prompting on an enormous scale and the film must not present unwilling compliance as either innocent or guilty.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a settlement is not a description. A quarrel a thousand years old ended, and what came out of it and survived is a list of what may and may not be done — when a monk may go to the village, what he must learn, that he may not carry another monastery's dispute outside it. None of that is a report on anybody's mind, and the old books say why no such report is possible: the factors a quarrel gets accused of arrive one at a time and exclude each other, so they can never be one state, and nothing about which of them is present is visible from outside. The viewer could come away holding the difference between conduct, which can be regulated and carved, and whatever was actually going on in the people, which cannot — and holding it from a rock face rather than from an assertion.
what_must_be_real: The rock, the writing and the light. Nothing on the inscription may be chalked, wetted, powdered, brushed, raked with an added lamp, traced, or sharpened in the grade to make it legible; if it does not read in the light the day supplies, the film shows it not reading and the voice says so. No reconstruction, overlay, animated transcription or superimposed translation appears on the stone. The images are filmed as they stand, under whatever shelter is there, and the shelter is in shot rather than hidden. This is a living place of worship with constant visitors: no act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repositioned or lit for filming; no monk, pilgrim or visitor is an exhibit, and nobody in frame is presented as devout, composed, attained, or — since this group's concepts are the unwholesome factors — as angry, envious, proud or grasping. People appear as passage at the edge of the frame, never as illustration, and anyone recognisable is filmed only where they can meaningfully refuse. The expelled monks of the record are named in the film only as the record names them: numbers and a procedure, not characters. No fraternity is ranked and no tradition is presented as the correct one. The wording quoted from the inscription is quoted from a published translation and attributed to it, never presented as our own reading of the stone.
position_hint: late middle: it is the group's coldest and most static film and the one that dismantles the group's own vocabulary, so it works best after two or three films have established what these factors are said to be. It also wants to sit after at least one film in which something is unmistakably felt, so that the refusal to read a mind lands as restraint rather than as evasion. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Alleging. The whole film is built on words for faults, and the moment the voice attaches one of them to a named fraternity, an elder, a king or a monk, it has broken the digest's central limit that no factor is readable from outside. The narration names the factors only as what the sources define and what a dispute would be accused of, never as what anybody had.

Framing a living worshipper or visitor as an instance of an unwholesome state. A camera cannot show which factor is present and this group's concepts make the temptation acute; nobody in frame may be read as angry, envious, proud, grasping or composed.

Ranking the three fraternities, or letting the unified order read as the correct one. This series' sources come from the tradition that prevailed, and that is a reason for care and not for triumph: the chronicle and the inscription are both documents of the winning side, and the film says so rather than narrating their account as neutral history.

Dramatising the expulsions. Monks were removed from the order and the record says so; the film states it once, plainly, and does not call it a purge, does not imply the expelled deserved it, and does not imply they were wronged. Nothing is known here about any individual.

Narrating the king's merit, piety or statesmanship. The council, the code and the carving are evidence that something was organised, not a verdict on anybody's virtue. The inscription's own first-person self-description — a mighty emperor who cannot remain indifferent — is quoted once as the stone's wording and is immediately marked as such; quoted any other way it becomes praise.

Making the inscription legible by intervention. Chalk, water, flour, raking lights, wet-plate tricks, photogrammetric relief renders and aggressive grading are all off the table on a World Heritage surface, and the film's honesty depends on the panel reading or not reading in available light.

The modern shelter. It keeps the weather off the carving and it takes away most of the raking light the macro work needs; whether the inscribed panel sits under it at all was not established in desk research. If the light is not there, the film is a film about writing that cannot be read, which is a different and still workable piece — but the treatment has to be decided before a crew is booked.
Letting the viewer hear stinginess as greed, which is exactly the equation the sources refuse: it grows from attachment to one's own but arises with aversion, as displeasure at sharing [C026-M:L19].
Letting the viewer hear envy as a variety of anger. Envy, stinginess and remorse each need aversion but are distinct factors and only one is present at a time [C026-P:L39].

Implying that monks who complied unwillingly were thereby innocent. Prompted unwholesome minds are fully unwholesome; prompting changes the texture, not the moral quality [C026-P:L43]. The film neither excuses nor accuses unwilling compliance.

Implying that the parties to the dispute were a type of person. The four constant factors describe every unwholesome moment in anyone and do not describe a kind of person [C026-M:L15]; the film must not sort the historical parties into the corrupt and the disciplined.

Building anything on the four-aspect wording of stinginess where the two sources disagree. The digest flags Margaya's fourth aspect as possibly an OCR error for 'hiding' rather than 'indicating' and says it needs checking against the print [C022-M:L43], so the film uses only the five kinds and the object-direction, both of which are clear.

Touching the three directions of conceit at all. 'I am inferior' is classed as conceit [C022-P:L111] and the digest forbids using that to moralise about low self-worth, and the description of equal-conceit contains egalitarian-sounding statements that would badly mislead if quoted in a film about three houses being made one [C022-P:L109]. The voice stays with superiority-conceit's named measures and goes no further.
Treating brooding regret as purification, which Pradeepika explicitly rejects [C022-P:L143]. Nothing in the film invites the viewer to feel usefully bad about anything.

Drone. A World Heritage site where flight needs clearance from several authorities at once, and a rock face is a ground subject in any case. The film is planned with no aerial footage and loses nothing if permission is refused.

Overlapping the group's own films. The treatment is the guard: one surface, no landscape, no water, no movement, no crowd as subject. If a cut starts wanting an establishing aerial or a wider world, the film has drifted.
drop_if: The inscribed panel cannot be approached closely enough for macro work without crossing a rope line or standing where worshippers need to be.
Filming on the terrace cannot be done without interrupting, restarting or repositioning worship, or without people who cannot refuse a camera being unavoidably identifiable.
The only way to get the writing on screen is to intervene on the surface, or to composite a transcription over it.
The colossal images and the inscribed panel cannot in fact be held in one frame, which is the shot the whole film is built on.

connections.note: Stay clear. That film is at the same ancient capital and turns on the same king's works, and its subject is one name over a thing that is counted two ways — five basins or three, both correct. Nothing about water, scale, counting, or a name laid over an assemblage belongs in this film, and no shot of that reservoir, its bund or its sluices appears here. This film is a dry rock face and a rulebook, it never leaves one surface, it has no aerial work at all, and its story is not the king's engineering but the ending of a monastic division. Where the two records touch — the same reign, the same chronicle — this film takes only the council and the code.

Stay clear. That film is a colonnade and a stupa in the older capital, and its what_is_disputed already records the origins of the monastic division — the episode in which an earlier king is said to have acted against the older community and a rival monastery was founded. This film must not narrate those origins: its story is the division's ending, roughly a thousand years later, and the fraternities are named once, neutrally, without a founding narrative and without ranking. That film's method is a walk between two monuments and two failure modes of a name; this one never moves off a single face, and what it watches is not a name but a list of prohibitions.

The group's other film about a written rule governing conduct in advance: there, a rotation that decides where water goes for a hundred kilometres; here, a code that decides when a monk may walk to a village. That film is in motion the whole way and this one never moves, and the water film's rules are still being obeyed while this one's have been unenforceable for eight hundred years.

The other film in the group about something that cannot be seen from outside while it is happening. There, a sealed kiln burning for nights with no way to look in; here, a record that never contained the thing anyone wants to know. One is an inside that exists and is hidden; the other is an inside that was never written down.

selection.reason: It is the group's only film whose subject is writing, the only one that never leaves a single surface, and the only one carrying a chronicled and inscribed historical story rather than a working place that resembles the concept. It is also the film that takes the group's own vocabulary of faults and shows that it cannot be applied to a record, which the group needs somewhere in it.

review.note: Rewritten completely on 2026-09-25 and the older verdict is void, because the film, the place and the argument are all new. The previous version was a wet-zone palm-tapping hillside: a good working place, but eleven of this group's fourteen candidates were working places carrying no historical story, and Chathura has ruled that a group may not be a monoculture, so the weakest occupants of that cell are the ones to replace. This one is bound to a documented history instead of a resemblance. The location is a single rock face at a ruined medieval capital, carrying four colossal twelfth-century images and, between two of them, a fifty-one-line inscription in medieval Sinhala: the katikāvata of Parākramabāhu I, a code of monastic conduct drawn up with the elders after a congregation of monks conventionally dated to 1165, when a division of the order into three fraternities that the stone itself reckons at one thousand two hundred and fifty-four years was brought to an end. The film's argument is that a quarrel is exactly where the fourteen unwholesome factors of C022 would be alleged to live, that C026's rules of combination make such an allegation arithmetically impossible as a single state, and that what survives on the rock is therefore not a record of anybody's mind but a list of what may and may not be done — with the limit stated on screen rather than in a note, since the code itself forbids speaking ill of anyone who performs the duties unwillingly. The expulsions are recorded once, plainly, neither dramatised nor adjudicated; the three fraternities are named once and not ranked, and the fact that this series' sources come from the tradition that prevailed is written into the risks. Both concepts were re-read from the digests for this rewrite and every citation was checked against the source lines it carries. The treatment is deliberately unlike anything else in the group: one surface, raking light and macro, locked-off frames, no landscape, no drone, no payoff shot of scenery. Two GRP-01 films sit close to this one — the great reservoir at the same ancient city and the colonnade-and-stupa film that already records the division's origins — and both are held off with explicit connections entries.

suggested_location.name: The katikāvata rock inscription at Gal Vihara (the Uttarārāma), with the colossal images on the same face, Polonnaruwa

also_known_as.name: Uttarārāma
also_known_as.used_by: the name used in the twelfth century and in the Cūḷavaṃsa

also_known_as.name: katikāvata
also_known_as.meaning: a code or covenant of monastic conduct agreed between the king and the elders
also_known_as.used_by: Sinhala usage; the standing term for this class of document

also_known_as.name: Vijjadhara Guhā / Vidyādhara Guhā
also_known_as.meaning: the cave of the bearers of knowledge
also_known_as.used_by: applied by different sources to different parts of the face; see what_is_disputed

suggested_location.region: Polonnaruwa District, North Central Province: the northern end of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa, inside the walled archaeological zone, about a kilometre and a half north of the citadel and the quadrangle
suggested_location.why_here: Because the film's whole argument is cut into one surface, at two scales, by one work programme. On this face stand four colossal twelfth-century images in the living rock, and between the cave shrine and the standing figure a rectangle of the same rock was polished and then filled with fifty-one lines of medieval Sinhala: a code of monastic discipline drawn up by named elders after a congregation of monks, at the end of a division of the order the inscription itself reckons at more than twelve hundred years. That is not a place that resembles the concept. It is the settlement of a thousand-year quarrel, written down as rules, on the same stone as the images — which is precisely the distinction the two concepts turn on, between a state of mind that arrives one flicker at a time and is invisible from outside, and a list of permissions that can be carved and enforced. The single most valuable frame the place produces is also the clearest statement of the argument: a standing figure of nearly seven metres and, two paces to its right, letters a few millimetres high, on one rock, in one shot. And the site imposes the film's discipline for it, because there is nothing else here to shoot: no landscape, no water, no horizon, no skyline, and a shelter overhead that rules out the sky. A film that cannot leave one surface is exactly the film this group needs and does not have.
what_to_film: The single establishing frame the whole film rests on: the standing figure and the inscribed panel in one locked-off shot, wide enough to show that they are the same rock and close enough that the writing reads as writing.
The inscribed panel at an oblique angle in the first low light after the site opens, so that the cutting lifts out of the grain, and the same panel square on at midday when it goes flat and vanishes.
Macro on the script: a line, then a word, then one letter deep enough to show the lit wall and the dark floor of the stroke, with dust and lichen in the cut.
The edge of the polished rectangle, where the worked surface stops and the raw granite begins — the boundary between a made document and the rock it was made on.

The colossal images in flat shade at the same lens lengths used for the letters, so the cut between the largest and the smallest thing on the face is a cut between comparable frames and not between a wide and a close-up.
The cave shrine's doorway and the standing figure as the two things the inscription lies between, filmed as the panel's neighbours rather than as monuments in their own right.
The modern shelter, in shot and unhidden: its posts, its shade line on the paving, and the way the usable light arrives sideways underneath it.
The terrace as passage only: bare feet on hot pale paving, shoes left at the line, offerings set down and removed — nobody held, nobody characterised, no worship as spectacle.
The closing move: one continuous pull from a single letter to the whole face, ending on the opening frame with the panel gone blank.
suggested_location.access: Inside the Polonnaruwa archaeological zone, which is a UNESCO World Heritage property administered together by the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund. A single site ticket bought at the museum near the main entrance covers all the monuments; foreign adult admission is reported at about USD 25, and gates reported as opening at 07:00, which is the window the film's first light depends on. The face is reached on a short walk from a car park at the northern end of the zone; there is no climb. It is a living place of worship as well as a monument: shoes and hats off at the line, shoulders and knees covered, a rope line in front of the images, and signs asking visitors not to turn their backs on the figures for photographs. Any tripod work, any extended presence on the terrace, and any macro work close to the rock will need permission from the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund, and probably supervision. Drone flight over an archaeological site of this class requires clearance from the Civil Aviation Authority, the Department of Archaeology, the Central Cultural Fund and the police; treat it as doubtful, and note that the subject is a vertical ground surface under a roof, so nothing is lost. None of this has been verified with any authority.
suggested_location.best_time: Two windows on the same day, for two different things. The first hour or so after the gates open, for low light reaching in sideways under the shelter and crossing the inscribed panel at a shallow enough angle for the cutting to read; and the last hour or so of the afternoon for the same effect from the other side, plus warm bounce off the paving onto the images. The middle of the day is for the figures in flat shade and for the writing at its most invisible, which the film needs as well. The dry months give the hardest, cleanest light; the north-east monsoon around November and December is the wettest period here and the least useful. Weekends, full-moon poya days and the pilgrimage season bring far more people, and the film wants the quiet end of that, not the crowd.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research done on 25 September 2026 by web search and by reading one primary edition online; nothing has been checked on the ground, against a print edition, or with any authority. The inscription's text is not paraphrased from secondary accounts: the transcript and Wickremasinghe's English translation were read in full from the Zenodo copy of the Siddham record IN03104, which reproduces 'No. 41. (Reg. No. 278.) Poḷonnaruva, Gal-Vihāra: Rock-Inscription of Parakkama-Bāhu I', Epigraphia Zeylanica 2, pp. 256-283. Every provision quoted or summarised in this record — the two divisions marked by fish symbols, the historical section in lines 1 to 18 and the injunctions in lines 18 to 51, the texts to be learnt by heart, the six-monthly examination, the restriction on entering the village and its exceptions, the requirement of a letter or an emissary before a monk from another community is lodged, the daily timetable, the rules on anger and on laughter, the rule against carrying another monastery's dispute outside it, the rule against coveting even permitted requisites, the examination before ordination, the rule that no ill is to be spoken of anyone who performs these duties unwillingly, and the three-warnings-then-expulsion procedure — comes from that translation and can be checked line by line. The headline point about the image of the site is this: NO photograph of the inscription itself could be found on Wikimedia Commons. The whole 'Gal Viharaya' category was listed, 136 files were checked file by file against their titles and descriptions for any mention of an inscription, a sellipiya or a katikāvata, and there is none; keyword searches for the inscription, for katikāvata and for Polonnaruwa rock inscriptions return only digitised books. Wikimedia's image servers refuse direct downloads to this agent, so no candidate image could be inspected visually, and for that reason no picture here is captioned as showing the inscription and the general view is explicitly disclaimed. All five files were confirmed to exist through action=query&titles= with the descriptive user agent, and their licences are as printed in the captions. The physical description of the panel is thin and partly historical: 51 lines and the two-part division are from the Siddham record and lankapradeepa; the only measurement found anywhere is Lieutenant Fagon's account of 1820, quoted by amazinglanka, that 'between the door and the standing figure, the rock is made smooth for about 6 ft. square, and this space is covered with a close written Kandian [sic] inscription perfectly legible'. No modern measurement of the panel, no letter height, no depth of cutting and no conservation assessment of its present legibility was found, and the description of the letters as a few millimetres deep is an inference from fifty-one lines in a panel of that size and is NOT sourced. That Fagon found it perfectly legible in 1820 is not evidence about its condition in 2026. The protective shelter is reported by several travel and heritage sources, one of which dates it to the 1960s while another calls it new; the date is unverified, and crucially it was not established whether the inscribed panel sits under the shelter or outside its span. Since the film's macro work depends on raking light, that is the first thing a pre-visit must settle, and it is listed in the risks and the unknowns. Access, ticket price, opening time, dress and photography rules are from travel and operator sources and are unverified. Drone requirements are from drone-law summaries, not from the authorities. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage property (Ancient City of Polonnaruwa, inscribed 1982) and no filming or research permission of any kind has been sought.

historical_thread.story:
The rock face is the surviving part of a twelfth-century monastery called the Uttarārāma, the northern monastery, at the northern edge of Polonnaruwa, and it was made under Parākramabāhu I, who reigned from 1153 to 1186. Four images were cut from the living rock — a large seated figure, a small seated figure inside an excavated cave, a standing figure with its arms crossed on its chest, and a reclining figure — and between the cave and the standing figure a rectangle of the same rock was ground flat and polished and then inscribed, in medieval Sinhala, with fifty-one lines divided into two parts, each ending in a fish symbol. The inscription is the katikāvata of Parākramabāhu I: a code of monastic conduct. It was published by Don Martino de Zilva Wickremasinghe as No. 41, Reg. No. 278, in Epigraphia Zeylanica 2, pages 256 to 283, and both the transcript and his English translation can be read in full.

The stone tells its own history first. It counts 454 years from the Buddha's death to the reign of Vaḷagam Abhā, and then 1254 years during which, in Wickremasinghe's translation, 'the Buddhist Fraternity remained disintegrated, and the religion also continued its course of decadence'. The order had long been divided into three fraternities, the Mahāvihāra, the Abhayagiri and the Jetavana. The stone then has the king reason in the first person: 'Seeing over and over again a blot such as this on the immaculate Buddhist religion, if a mighty emperor like myself were to remain indifferent, the Buddhist religion would perish... Let me serve the Buddhist religion which should last five thousand years.' It records that he turned to the community of monks of the Udumbaragiri monastery, in the forest-dwelling tradition, headed by Mahā Kāśyapa Mahā-sthavira, and that — expressly on the model of Aśoka enlisting Moggaliputta Tissa to crush out sinful bhikkhus, suppress heretics, purge the religion and hold the Third Rehearsal of the Dhamma — he 'removing from the Master's religion many hundreds of sinful monks, brought about a rapprochement of the three fraternities and a coalition of them into one single fraternity — a reconciliation which former kings, despite their great efforts, were not able to effect'. It then records the elders' own part: having heard the king's repeated appeals, the community of theras headed by Mahā Kassapa 'formulated the following code of disciplinary injunctions without deviating from the customary formalities observed in the lineage of preceptors, and after due consultation of the Dhamma and the Vinaya, in order that those of negligent conduct may not find an opening'. The congregation behind it is conventionally dated to 1165. The Cūḷavaṃsa, the chronicle's continuation, covers the same reform in its seventy-eighth chapter.

The second part of the inscription, lines 18 to 51, is the code, and it is unexpectedly domestic. Heads of chapters are told not to let their co-residents and pupils neglect study, and the texts they must learn are named: the Kudusikha and the Pāmok from the Vinaya literature, the three Dasadhamma-suttas and the Anumāna-sutta from the Suttanta. Those who cannot master a long course must at least learn the Mulsikha and the Sekhiyā by heart and rehearse the Sikhavaḷan̆da-vinisa, and be able to repeat any part of it correctly when questioned every six months. Novices have their own list. Then the day: sleep at midnight, rise at dawn, walk and meditate through the morning, rehearse a learnt text, put on the robe properly, clean the teeth, attend to the duties owed to the dāgabas, the bodhi tree, the terrace, the preceptors, the elders, the sick and the lodgings, take the gruel, and go back to meditation; and after the midday meal the same, without consorting with lay or monastic society until duties fall due. Then the boundaries. No permission to enter the village at wrong times on any business whatsoever, except to beg food for unsupported parents, for consanguineous and widowed sisters and for fellow monks, or to get medicine in illness, or to go and recite the Paritta at an appointed place; an unlearned monk may not be given leave unaccompanied, and the preceptor who grants it commits an offence; a monk arriving from another community is not to be lodged without a letter or an emissary from the head of the place he came from. At all times monks are to refrain from inappropriate words with anyone, whether in anger or in fun; they are not to be angry with servants without first putting the matter to the elders; they are not to give away anything of their own without the elders' permission; even where there is just cause for laughter they are to show it with mouths closed; disputes being settled in a monastery one has entered are not to be made known outside, and one is not to take up another monastery's disputes; they are not to be covetous even of requisites the Vinaya allows them; they are not to talk while worshipping, offering, using the tooth-stick or putting the bowl away; they are not to brush against senior monks with their bodies or their robes, nor stand too near, nor sway their arms, nor stroke a boy's head, nor at any place put their arms round a boy's body to console him. Admission, higher ordination and the grant of nissaya protection are all to be made only after examination. And then, two lines from the end, this: 'No ill shall be spoken [of any one] for unwillingly observing these aforesaid duties.' The last provisions are the sanctions. A monk who disobeys is punished and warned; when that has happened three times running and he still behaves the same way, he is refused nissaya, allowed to remain a month, and then, if his conduct is still not in accordance with the Vinaya, expelled, and no one is to keep company with him. Theras who are heads of chapters and fail to bring their communities under discipline are themselves punished as the senior theras determine.

What happened afterwards is a matter of record and of reading. The two abolished fraternities do not reappear as orders; the later Sri Lankan sangha descends from the Mahāvihāra tradition. Richard Gombrich's account of what 'reunited' means is blunter than the chronicle's: the king abolished the Abhayagiri and Jetavana Nikāyas, laicised many monks of the Mahāvihāra and all the monks of the other two, and then allowed the better ones among the latter to become novices in the now unified sangha. Katikāvatas went on being made. Parākramabāhu II of Dambadeniya, in the thirteenth century, promulgated one that took parts of this text into itself, and the series of them runs on to Rājādhi Rājasiṃha at the end of the eighteenth century. By the eighteenth century the ordination line had lapsed altogether and had to be brought back from Siam; and new fraternities were founded after that — the Siyam Nikāya in the eighteenth century, the Amarapura in 1800, the Rāmañña in the nineteenth, the last two merging again in 2019.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C022's list and C026's rules of combination ask one question between them, and this rock face is where that question was actually answered in public: what can be written down about a quarrel?

The first binding is the vocabulary. Read C022 fresh and four of its fourteen factors are defined in terms that a dispute between three monastic houses fits without any pushing. Envy takes other people's prosperity and standing as its object, and the Pradeepika's description of it includes disparaging those who keep precepts and meditate by presenting their virtue as hypocrisy and as a device for getting gifts and honours — which is the standard content of every accusation ever made in a religious quarrel. Stinginess takes one's own as its object, and the five things it is said to fasten on are a dwelling, a following, a gain, appearance and the teaching itself: a monastery, a lineage, an endowment, a reputation and a doctrine, which is an inventory of exactly what the three fraternities each had. Conceit is mis-measuring one's own standing, and among the named measures are birth, merit, and one's own morality and concentration — the very ground a dispute about discipline stands on. Wrong view is the habit of holding matters contrary to reason and conditions, which is what each side in a doctrinal dispute says of the other. So the concept does not have to be imported here. It is already the language in which this history would be told, by anyone inclined to tell it that way.

The second binding is the refusal, and it is what makes the place right rather than merely apt. Nothing on this rock tells that story. The stone's own historical section is two-thirds royal self-presentation and one-third arithmetic: 454 years, 1254 years, a blot on the religion, hundreds of sinful monks removed, three fraternities made one, a code formulated after consultation of the Dhamma and the Vinaya so that the negligent may find no opening. Not one sentence of it is about what anybody felt. And the code itself, the thirty-odd lines that took the most stone, is entirely about conduct: which texts by heart, tested every six months; when the village may be entered and for whose sake; a letter before a stranger is lodged; sleep at midnight, rise at dawn; not angry with a servant without going to the elders; laughter with the mouth closed; another monastery's dispute not carried outside. That is a schedule of permissions. It is evidence, and strong evidence, that a dispute existed and that somebody with authority wanted it not to recur. It is no evidence at all about what was in anyone.

The third binding is C026, and it is what turns that observation into an argument instead of a caution. The combination rules are strict. All fourteen factors occur only in twelve minds and nowhere among the other seventy-seven. Four are in every single one of those twelve. Conceit and wrong view can never be in one mind, because they are two different grips — this is how things are, against this is how I rank. Envy, stinginess and remorse each require aversion, occur only occasionally, and never arrive two at a time. Put that against the accusation and the accusation dissolves as a description of a state: a quarrel called envious and grasping and proud and doctrinally fixed cannot be any single mind, because the sources say those cannot co-occur. It can only have been an enormous number of momentary, mutually exclusive states, arriving one flicker at a time in an enormous number of people over twelve hundred years. The combination the sources describe is fine-grained and invisible. The combination the rock records is administrative: a list, a procedure, a sanction. The film's central cut — from a field of small letters to a figure nearly seven metres high, on the same stone — is the two orders of magnitude the concept needs, and it exists here physically.

The fourth binding is the one that would be too good to be true if it were not in the published translation. Two lines before the sanctions, the code says: no ill shall be spoken of anyone for unwillingly observing these aforesaid duties. The document that regulates the conduct explicitly forbids inferring anything from the conduct about the person doing it. That is the digests' own limit — 'a camera cannot show which factor is present', 'not a diagnostic tool', 'they do not describe a type of person' — cut into a rock in the twelfth century by the people who had the most reason to want the inference. And the exit the film takes at the end is also the sources' own: the Pradeepika distinguishes the unwholesome, hindering doubt from ordinary uncertainty about something one does not know, which may not be unwholesome at all. The film does not know what was in these minds. On the sources' own account, that particular not-knowing is not a fault.

One further thing binds, and it binds as a caution rather than as an argument. This series' own source texts belong to the tradition that prevailed in this settlement. The chronicle that praises the reform was continued by that tradition; the inscription was cut by its patron; and the two other fraternities left no comparable account. That asymmetry is a fact about the record and it is exactly the sort of asymmetry the film is about: what survives is what someone was in a position to carve. It is recorded and it is never used as a verdict.
what_is_certain: The four images and the inscription are on one rock face at the site called Gal Vihara, originally the Uttarārāma, at the northern end of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa, and the complex is attributed to Parākramabāhu I, who reigned 1153-1186 CE.

The inscription is carved on a flattened and polished part of the rock face between the cave shrine and the standing image, and it has 51 lines in two parts, each part ending in a fish symbol: lines 1-18 a historical introduction, lines 18-51 the disciplinary injunctions. The script and language are medieval Sinhala.

It was edited, transcribed and translated by Don Martino de Zilva Wickremasinghe as 'No. 41. (Reg. No. 278.) Poḷonnaruva, Gal-Vihāra: Rock-Inscription of Parakkama-Bāhu I (1153-1186 A.D.)', Epigraphia Zeylanica 2, pp. 256-283.

The inscription's own reckoning: 454 years from the Buddha's passing to the reign of Vaḷagam Abhā, and thereafter 1254 years during which, in Wickremasinghe's translation, 'the Buddhist Fraternity remained disintegrated, and the religion also continued its course of decadence'.
The order was divided into three fraternities, the Mahāvihāra, the Abhayagiri and the Jetavana.

The inscription quotes the king in the first person, in Wickremasinghe's translation: 'Seeing over and over again a blot such as this on the immaculate Buddhist religion, if a mighty emperor like myself were to remain indifferent, the Buddhist religion would perish, and many living beings will be destined to the apāya. Let me serve the Buddhist religion which should last five thousand years.'

The inscription names the monks whose services were enlisted as the community resident in the Udumbaragiri monastery, headed by Mahā Kāśyapa Mahā-sthavira, and expressly takes Aśoka's enlistment of Moggaliputta Tissa as its model.

The expulsions as the inscription itself characterises them, in Wickremasinghe's translation: the king, enlisting those monks and 'removing from the Master's religion many hundreds of sinful monks, brought about a rapprochement of the three fraternities and a coalition of them into one single fraternity (nikāya) - a reconciliation which former kings, despite their great efforts, were not able to effect'. No number beyond 'many hundreds' is given, and no individual is named among them.

The inscription attributes the drafting to the monks and not to the king: 'the Community of Theras, headed by the great Thera Mahā Kassapa, formulated the following code of disciplinary injunctions without deviating from the customary formalities observed in the lineage of preceptors, and after due consultation of the Dhamma and the Vinaya, in order that those of negligent conduct may not find an opening [for transgression].'

What the code prescribes, from the published translation: named texts to be learnt (the Kudusikha and Pāmok from the Vinaya, the three Dasadhamma-suttas and the Anumāna-sutta from the Suttanta; for weaker students the Mulsikha, the Sekhiyā and the Sikhavaḷan̆da-vinisa, to be repeatable on questioning every six months; the Heraṇasikha, Sekhiyā and Dasadhamma-sutta for novices); a daily timetable (sleep at midnight, rise at dawn, walk and meditate, rehearse, robe, clean the teeth, the Khandaka duties in respect of the dāgabas, the bodhi tree, the terrace, preceptors, theras, the sick and the lodgings, gruel, then meditation; the same after the midday meal); and a list of prohibitions and permissions.

Specific provisions, from the same translation: no permission to enter the village at wrong times on any business whatsoever, except a journey to beg food for unsupported parents, consanguineous and widowed sisters and co-followers of the religious life, or to procure or beg medicine in illness, or to recite the Paritta at an appointed place; no leave for an unlearned monk unaccompanied, and the preceptor who grants it commits a dukkaṭa offence; no lodging for a monk from another community without a letter or an emissary from the head thera of his former place; no inappropriate words with anyone in anger or in fun; no anger with servants without first complaining to the elders; nothing of one's own given away without the elders' permission; mirth only with closed mouth; disputes being settled in a monastery one has entered not to be made known outside, and another monastery's disputes not to be taken up; no covetousness even for requisites the Vinaya allows; no talking while worshipping, offering, using the tooth-stick or casing the bowl; no brushing against senior monks with body or robe, no standing too near, no swaying the arms, no stroking a boy's head and never putting one's arms round a boy's body to console him; admission, upasampadā and nissaya all to be conferred only after examination.
The code contains the provision, two lines from its end in Wickremasinghe's translation: 'No ill shall be spoken [of any one] for unwillingly observing these aforesaid duties.'

The sanctions, from the same translation: a monk who disobeys receives the punishment due and is warned; when this has been done three times successively and he continues in the same way he is refused nissaya, allowed to remain a month, and if his demeanour is still not in accordance with the Vinaya he is to be expelled and no one is to hold communion with him; theras who head chapters and fail to bring their communities under discipline receive the punishments determined by the senior theras.

Katikāvatas do not alter the canonical Vinaya; they add rules intended to secure its observance. Parākramabāhu II of Dambadeniya in the thirteenth century promulgated a katikāvata that incorporated parts of this text, and the documented series of them continues to Rājādhi Rājasiṃha (1782-98).

The Abhayagiri and Jetavana nikāyas do not appear as orders in the later record; the later Sri Lankan sangha descends from the Mahāvihāra tradition. The fraternities that exist today were founded much later: the Siyam Nikāya in the mid-eighteenth century after the higher ordination was brought back from Siam, the Amarapura in 1800, the Rāmañña in the nineteenth century, and the Amarapura and Rāmañña merged on 16 August 2019.
The reform is also covered by the Cūḷavaṃsa, the continuation of the chronicle, in its seventy-eighth chapter.
A modern metal shelter stands over the rock face to protect the carving from weathering, and the site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage property 'Ancient City of Polonnaruwa', inscribed in 1982.
what_is_disputed: The date of the congregation. 1165 is given everywhere in the secondary literature, but the transcript and translation read for this record contain no regnal year and no date at all: the only numbers in the inscription's own reckoning are 454 and 1254. Those two, added, give 1708 years from the Buddha's passing, which on the traditional era falls in the mid-1160s — so the conventional date appears to be an inference from the stone's arithmetic rather than a reading of a date on the stone. That arithmetic is this record's own and is not attributed to any scholar. Treat 1165 as the conventional date, not as an inscribed one.

Whether the inscription is 'one of the longest inscriptions from ancient Sri Lanka', as one source calls it, cannot be reconciled with the only measurement found, Lieutenant Fagon's 1820 note that the smoothed space is 'about 6 ft. square'. Either the panel is small and densely written, or Fagon measured part of it, or the superlative is loose. Fifty-one lines is firm; the extent is not.

The present legibility of the panel. Fagon in 1820 called it 'perfectly legible'; no modern condition report was found, and no letter height, cutting depth or conservation assessment could be located. Nothing here establishes that it can be read today, and the film is built to state that rather than assume it.

The names of the parts of the face. Wikipedia calls the cave shrine the Vidyādhara Guhā; lankapradeepa applies Vijjadhara Guhā to the large seated image instead and calls the cave shrine the Nisinna-patima Lena. The naming is not settled between the sources consulted and the film does not rely on it.

The dimensions of the images do not agree. The seated image is given as 15 ft 2.5 in (4.636 m) and as 16 ft 3 in (4.98 m); the standing image as 22 ft 9 in (6.93 m) and as 'approximately 7 metres (23 ft)'; the reclining image as 46 ft 4 in (14.12 m) and, in one account, as 'approximately 24.4 metres (80 feet)', which cannot be reconciled with the first. Figures are reported as reported and none is treated as measured.

The identification of the standing image is a long-running scholarly dispute: H. C. P. Bell read it as Ānanda standing in mourning, and Paranavitāna and later scholars as the Buddha himself, variously in the para-dukkha-dukkhita attitude or paying homage to the bodhi tree in the third week after the enlightenment. This is recorded as a layer of the site's history and the film builds nothing on it; a disputed identification is another film's subject in this slate and does not belong here.

The shelter. Several sources report a protective roof; one dates it to the 1960s and another describes it as new. The date is unverified, and — the practical unknown that matters most — it was not established whether the inscribed panel lies under the shelter or beyond its span, which determines whether raking light on the letters exists at all.

What 'unification' means, and whether it lasted. The inscription and the chronicle present a rapprochement and a coalition into one fraternity that earlier kings could not achieve. Gombrich's reading is that the king abolished the Abhayagiri and Jetavana nikāyas, laicised many Mahāvihāra monks and all the monks of the other two, and then let the better ones among the latter re-enter as novices. Both statements are about the same events. What is not in dispute is that the two nikāyas do not reappear; what is unsettled is whether 'reconciliation' or 'abolition' is the better description, and the film records both without choosing. Nor is it established how long the code itself was observed: a further katikāvata within about eighty years that reuses this text, the later series down to the end of the eighteenth century, the lapse of the ordination line before it was brought back from Siam, and the founding of new fraternities in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries are all documented, but no record of this code's enforcement or of when it fell out of use was found.

The provenance of the whole account. The inscription was cut by the reform's patron and the chronicle was continued within the tradition that prevailed; the Abhayagiri and Jetavana left no comparable statement of their side. Everything above therefore describes what one party recorded. That is the character of the evidence and it is not adjudicated: the film does not rank the three fraternities, does not present the surviving tradition as the correct one, and does not treat the removal of monks as either deserved or unjust.

The exact wording of everything quoted here is Wickremasinghe's English, published between 1912 and 1927 and read online rather than in the printed volume. No Sinhala or Pali reading has been checked against the stone or against a second scholarly edition, and a translation of that date may not be how the text would be rendered now.

unknowns: Whether the inscribed panel can be read at all in available light today, and whether it lies under the modern shelter. This is the first thing a pre-visit must settle and it changes the film's macro strategy.
How close a camera can get to the panel, and whether tripod and macro work in front of the images is permitted at all.
Whether permission for extended filming can be obtained from the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund, and on what conditions.

No measurement of the panel, the letter height or the depth of the cutting was found; the film's key frame assumes the images and the writing can be held together and that has not been verified on the ground.

Whether a modern scholarly edition or re-translation of the inscription exists that would supersede Wickremasinghe's, and whether an expert reader should be consulted before any wording is quoted on screen.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified; the inscription's content is read from a published translation online and not from the stone or the printed volume. No scene or shot is decided here.
